title: Equally Accurate, or Equally Fast
scopeNote: This keeps the diffusion model, the caution control and the joint speed-accuracy plot. The discrimination task the learner performs is not included: the original's own notes state that the simulator reaches every conclusion on the page without it and offer it there as the non-timed route, so this edition keeps the route that carries the argument. Practice blocks, three contrasting strategies and a difficulty control stay in the longer version.
summary: Two fictional people on the same task, one better at it at every speed. Move one dial and they look identical on accuracy, move it again and they look identical on time.
learningObjectives: Explain why one outcome measure cannot separate task performance from response caution.
Distinguish where somebody sits on their curve from which curve they are on.
Explain why a faster person at equal accuracy has not been shown to be better.
Recognise that reading speed as caution is the same error as reading it as ability.
interactionTypes: a prediction about what a faster response at equal accuracy establishes
a live control over one person's response caution
accuracy and time reported together and recomputed on every move
both people's whole speed-accuracy curves plotted at once
a guided toggle between the equal-accuracy and equal-time settings
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. No task is performed, nothing is timed, and nothing measures the reader.
accessibilityNotes: Nothing on the page is timed and there is no performed task, so no speeded response is required of anyone. Caution is a native range input reporting its value in text, and every figure in the chart is also a readout tile carrying accuracy and time together in words. Each person's marker is labelled by name, with a paint-order halo so it stays legible where a gridline runs behind it, and the chart description states which curve dominates and gives both current positions. The tile that reports what looks the same says so in words and carries a non-colour state signal. There is no motion.
dataStatus: Two fictional people whose behaviour is produced by a formula. Nothing is measured, and what differs between them is how clearly this task's evidence arrives for each, which is a property of a person meeting a task rather than a general ability.
simulationNotes: The model is the standard closed form for a simple unbiased diffusion process: accuracy is the logistic of twice the drift times the threshold, and mean time is the non-decision time plus the threshold over the drift times the hyperbolic tangent of their product. Raising the threshold raises accuracy and raises time together, one dial moving two outcomes, which is the difficulty being taught. The two drift rates differ, 0.90 against 0.60, and the consequence, verified rather than assumed, is that the two speed-accuracy curves never cross: the first person is more accurate at every time and faster at every accuracy, so there is a fact of the matter about who does this task better. Yet the second person's caution alone decides which of two false impressions the data give: at 1.80 both are 89.7 per cent correct and the first is 1.32 seconds faster, and at 1.10 both take 1.36 seconds and the first is 10.8 points more accurate. The drift rates and the fixed caution were chosen by search so that both matching points land exactly on a step the slider can hold and agree to the displayed precision; two numbers count as the same on this page when they display the same, not when they fall inside a tolerance, so the page can never declare a match the reader can see is not one. Simplifications: this pair was chosen so that one dominates, where real curves frequently cross; caution is treated as a dial somebody sets, where in practice it responds to instructions, fatigue and stakes; and the model has no error term, so it gives points rather than estimates with uncertainty.
readmeTopic: why a score and a reaction time have to be read together or not at all
